title: Early voting is surging in Georgia suburbs. Rural counties tell another story. - The Atlanta Journal-Constitution
text:

 Politics Early voting surges in Georgia suburbs. Rural counties tell another story.
 Democratic and Republican strongholds around Atlanta are posting big gains over 2022. But many rural counties are struggling to keep pace. Share People walk into the Metropolitan Library in Atlanta on Tuesday, Oct. 20, 2026, during early voting for the Georgia general election. (Jason Getz/AJC) By Greg Bluestein and Charles Minshew Updated 15 hours ago Georgia’s early voting surge is fueled by a growing geographic divide, with voters in metro Atlanta’s suburbs and other more populous areas casting ballots well ahead of their 2022 pace while much of rural Georgia lags behind.
 According to an AJC analysis of voter participation and election results data from the Secretary of State’s Office, in the 132 counties that Republican Donald Trump carried in 2024, early turnout is essentially flat compared with the same stage of the 2022 midterms. But in the 27 counties that voted for Kamala Harris, the number of ballots cast has jumped 9%.
 Related Story AJC poll: Bottoms, Jackson deadlocked in race for Georgia governor The Democratic strongholds of Cobb and Gwinnett counties are running about 15% ahead of the same stage of the last midterm election. The GOP bastions of Cherokee and Forsyth counties are experiencing even greater spikes. 
 Over in Augusta’s left-leaning Richmond County, early voting has soared 65% compared with the same point in 2022. And other important Democratic counties, including DeKalb and Fulton counties, are seeing modest gains compared with 2022. 
 But the picture is far different across stretches of rural Georgia, where Republicans must rely on commanding margins to counter Democratic strength in metro Atlanta. Early turnout is down by double digits in Coffee, Colquitt and Laurens counties.
 More than 1.1 million Georgians have already cast ballots, putting statewide participation about 5% ahead of the same stage in 2022, according to the vote-tracking GeorgiaVotes website. 
 The uneven pace offers another glimpse of the electorate taking shape ahead of the Nov. 3 election, when Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms faces Republican Rick Jackson for governor and Republican Mike Collins is challenging Democratic U.S. Sen. Jon Ossoff.
 Related Story AJC poll: Jon Ossoff leads Mike Collins in Georgia’s U.S. Senate race But the early figures come with major caveats.
 First, they show who has cast a ballot, not which candidates are getting them. And with split-ticket voting expected to play a significant role, strong turnout in partisan strongholds doesn’t necessarily mean those voters are supporting one party down the ballot. 
 And the early-voting surge doesn’t necessarily mean higher overall turnout. Some Georgians may simply be voting now rather than waiting until Election Day, when more Republicans traditionally vote.
 Still, the emerging patterns are drawing attention. Democratic strategist Fred Hicks said President Donald Trump’s visit last week may have cut both ways, energizing Republicans while also motivating Democrats to turn out.
 There’s another intriguing wrinkle that makes reading the tea leaves more challenging: A sizable share of early voters skipped the last midterm altogether, making it harder to model how they might vote.
 At least 190,000 Georgians who have voted early this year sat out the 2022 midterms, including a significant number in Gwinnett County. Statewide, roughly 40% of Hispanic early voters and one-third of Asian American early voters didn’t cast ballots in the last midterm election.
 Plus, the pool of eligible voters is about 5% larger this year than it was in 2022. Georgia had 7.8 million registered voters in 2022, compared with 8.2 million registered voters this year.
 Correction
 October 23, 2026 This story has been updated to correct the percentage increase of voter turnout in early voting for the 2026 midterms in the 27 counties that voted for Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election.
 Greg Bluestein Greg Bluestein is the Atlanta Journal Constitution's chief political reporter. He is also an author, TV analyst and co-host of the Politically Georgia podcast.
 Charles Minshew Charles Minshew is a deputy managing editor at The Atlanta Journal-Constitution
